prompt: In 1858, Kekulé and Couper independently proposed what about carbon in organic compounds?

choices.text: Carbon is tetravalent: it always forms four bonds
Carbon's four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron
choices.why: That was van 't Hoff and Le Bel's proposal, in 1874.

choices.text: Carbon atoms bond by sharing electron pairs
choices.why: The shared-electron (covalent) bond was proposed by G. N. Lewis in 1916.

choices.text: Carbon chains can double back to form rings
choices.why: Kekulé suggested rings later, in 1865.

explanation: In 1858, August Kekulé and Archibald Couper independently proposed that carbon is tetravalent in all organic compounds: it always forms four bonds when it joins other elements to form stable compounds.

prompt: What did Kekulé suggest in 1865?

choices.text: Carbon chains can double back on themselves to form rings
Carbon always forms four bonds
choices.why: That was his (and Couper's) 1858 proposal.

choices.text: Carbon's bonds have specific directions in space
choices.why: That was van 't Hoff and Le Bel, in 1874.

choices.text: Electrons are shared in covalent bonds
choices.why: That was G. N. Lewis, in 1916.

explanation: Kekulé also said carbon atoms can bond to one another to form chains, and in 1865 he suggested that carbon chains can double back on themselves to form rings of atoms.

prompt: What did van 't Hoff and Le Bel add to the picture of organic compounds in 1874?

choices.text: A third dimension: carbon's four bonds point in specific directions, toward the corners of a tetrahedron
The idea that carbon forms four bonds
choices.why: Kekulé and Couper had already proposed that in 1858.

choices.text: The idea that carbon atoms can form rings
choices.why: Kekulé suggested rings in 1865.

choices.text: The electron-dot structure
choices.why: Lewis structures come from G. N. Lewis's work on shared electrons, in 1916.

explanation: Until 1874 chemistry was viewed two-dimensionally. Van 't Hoff and Le Bel proposed that carbon's four bonds have specific spatial directions, and van 't Hoff suggested the four attached atoms sit at the corners of a regular tetrahedron with carbon in the center.

prompt: In a drawing of a tetrahedral carbon, what does a heavy wedged line represent?

choices.text: A bond coming out of the page toward the viewer
A bond going back behind the page
choices.why: That is shown by a dashed line.

choices.text: A bond in the plane of the page
choices.why: That is shown by a solid line.

choices.text: A double bond
choices.why: A wedge shows a bond's direction in three dimensions, not its order.

explanation: Solid lines are bonds in the plane of the page, the heavy wedged line is a bond coming out of the page toward the viewer, and the dashed line is a bond receding behind the page.

prompt: In a drawing of a tetrahedral carbon, what does a dashed line represent?

choices.text: A bond receding behind the page, away from the viewer
A bond coming out of the page toward the viewer
choices.why: That is shown by a heavy wedged line.

choices.text: A bond in the plane of the page
choices.why: That is shown by a solid line.

choices.text: A bond that is breaking
choices.why: In these drawings a dashed line shows direction: back behind the page.

explanation: The dashed line represents a bond going back behind the plane of the page, away from the viewer.

prompt: In a wedge-and-dash drawing of a tetrahedral carbon, what does a plain solid line represent?

choices.text: A bond in the plane of the page
A bond coming toward the viewer
choices.why: That is shown by a heavy wedged line.

choices.text: A bond going away from the viewer
choices.why: That is shown by a dashed line.

choices.text: A bond to hydrogen only
choices.why: Solid lines are used for any bond lying in the plane of the page.

explanation: Solid lines represent bonds in the plane of the page; with one wedge and one dash, two solid lines and the carbon show the tetrahedral shape.

prompt: Why do atoms bond together?

choices.text: The resulting compound is more stable and lower in energy than the separate atoms
Bonding absorbs energy, which stabilizes the atoms
choices.why: Bond formation releases energy; that loss of energy is what makes the compound more stable.

choices.text: Atoms always have to reach eight electrons
choices.why: Hydrogen is stable with two. The underlying reason is lower energy.

choices.text: Bonding increases the atoms' energy
choices.why: A compound forms because it is lower in energy than the separate atoms.

explanation: Atoms bond together because the compound that results is more stable and lower in energy than the separate atoms.

prompt: What happens to energy when a chemical bond forms?

choices.text: Energy is released, usually as heat
Energy is absorbed
choices.why: Energy is absorbed when a bond breaks. Making bonds always releases energy.

choices.text: No energy change occurs
choices.why: Bond formation always releases energy; that's why the compound is lower in energy.

choices.text: Energy is released only for ionic bonds
choices.why: Making any bond releases energy.

explanation: Energy, usually as heat, is always released and flows out of the chemical system when a bond forms. Making bonds always releases energy, and breaking bonds always absorbs it.

prompt: What happens to energy when a chemical bond breaks?

choices.text: Energy must be added to the system
Energy is released
choices.why: Energy is released when a bond forms. Breaking a bond absorbs energy.

choices.text: Energy is released only if the bond is weak
choices.why: Breaking any bond absorbs energy; weaker bonds simply need less.

choices.text: No energy change occurs
choices.why: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy.

explanation: Energy is added to the chemical system when a bond breaks: breaking bonds always absorbs energy.

prompt: What gives the noble gases in group 8A their special stability?

choices.text: Eight electrons in their outermost (valence) shell
Having no electrons in their valence shell
choices.why: Their valence shells are full, not empty: Ne (2 + 8), Ar (2 + 8 + 8).

choices.text: Having the same number of protons and neutrons
choices.why: Their stability comes from their electron arrangement, an octet in the valence shell.

choices.text: Forming strong ionic bonds
choices.why: Noble gases rarely bond at all; their stability comes from a filled valence shell.

explanation: Eight electrons (an electron octet) in an atom's outermost shell, or valence shell, impart special stability to the noble gases: Ne (2 + 8), Ar (2 + 8 + 8), Kr (2 + 8 + 18 + 8).

prompt: How does sodium (group 1A) reach a noble-gas configuration?

choices.text: By losing the single s electron from its valence shell to form a cation
By gaining seven electrons to complete its valence shell
choices.why: Losing one electron takes far less energy than gaining seven.

choices.text: By sharing one electron pair in a covalent bond
choices.why: Alkali metals like sodium form cations; sharing is how atoms near the middle of the table bond.

choices.text: By gaining one electron to form an anion
choices.why: Sodium loses an electron, forming Na^+; halogens like chlorine gain one.

explanation: Main-group elements tend to take on the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas. The alkali metals such as sodium do this by losing the single s electron from their valence shell to form a cation.

prompt: How does chlorine (group 7A) reach a noble-gas configuration?

choices.text: By gaining a p electron to fill its valence shell, forming an anion
By losing seven electrons
choices.why: Gaining one electron takes far less energy than losing seven.

choices.text: By losing one electron to form a cation
choices.why: Chlorine gains an electron, forming Cl^−; sodium is the one that loses an electron.

choices.text: By gaining two electrons
choices.why: Chlorine has seven valence electrons and needs only one more for an octet.

explanation: The halogens such as chlorine achieve a noble-gas configuration by gaining a p electron to fill their valence shell and form an anion.

prompt: What holds the ions together in a compound such as Na^+ Cl^−?

choices.text: The electrical attraction of unlike charges, an ionic bond
A shared pair of electrons
choices.why: That is a covalent bond, which forms between atoms that share rather than transfer electrons.

choices.text: Overlap of the two ions' valence orbitals
choices.why: Orbital overlap describes covalent bonding; ions are held by the attraction of opposite charges.

choices.text: Attraction between the two nuclei
choices.why: Both nuclei are positive and repel each other; it's the opposite charges of the ions that attract.

explanation: The ions in compounds like Na^+ Cl^− are held together by the electrical attraction of unlike charges, which we call an ionic bond.

prompt: Why is the bonding in methane, CH4, not ionic?

choices.text: It would take too much energy for carbon to gain or lose four electrons
Carbon has no valence electrons to give up
choices.why: Carbon has four valence electrons (2s^2 2p^2), but removing or adding four takes too much energy.

choices.text: Hydrogen can't form ions
choices.why: The reason given is about carbon: gaining or losing four electrons is too costly.

choices.text: Methane is a gas
choices.why: Being a gas doesn't decide the bond type; the energy of forming C^4+ or C^4− does.

explanation: It would take too much energy for carbon (1s^2 2s^2 2p^2) either to gain or lose four electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration. Instead carbon bonds by sharing electrons.

prompt: What is a covalent bond?

choices.text: A bond formed by two atoms sharing a pair of electrons
The attraction between a cation and an anion
choices.why: That is an ionic bond.

choices.text: The transfer of an electron from one atom to another
choices.why: Electron transfer produces ions; a covalent bond shares electrons.

choices.text: The attraction between two nuclei
choices.why: Covalent bonds hold atoms together through shared electrons attracted to both nuclei.

explanation: Instead of gaining or losing electrons, carbon bonds to other atoms by sharing them. This shared-electron bond, first proposed in 1916 by G. N. Lewis, is called a covalent bond.

prompt: Which of these is not called a molecule?

choices.text: Sodium chloride, NaCl
Methane, CH4
choices.why: Methane's atoms are held together by covalent bonds, so it is a molecule.

choices.text: Water, H2O
choices.why: Water is a neutral collection of covalently bonded atoms, a molecule.

choices.text: Ammonia, NH3
choices.why: Ammonia's atoms are covalently bonded, so it is a molecule.

explanation: A molecule is a neutral collection of atoms held together by covalent bonds. Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride are held together by ionic bonds and are not called molecules.

prompt: How many dots surround oxygen in its electron-dot (Lewis) symbol?
explanation: Dots represent valence-shell electrons. Oxygen has six valence electrons (2s^2 2p^4), so it has six dots.

prompt: How many valence electrons are shown in the electron-dot structure of chloromethane, CH3Cl?
explanation: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, each hydrogen 1 and chlorine 7: 4 + 3(1) + 7 = 14. Eight are in the four bonds and six are in chlorine's three lone pairs.

prompt: How many covalent bonds does a nitrogen atom usually form?
explanation: Nitrogen has five valence electrons (2s^2 2p^3) and needs three more to reach the neon configuration, so it forms three bonds.

prompt: How many covalent bonds does an oxygen atom usually form?
explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons (2s^2 2p^4), needs two more for an octet, and so forms two bonds.

prompt: How many covalent bonds does a halogen atom such as chlorine usually form?
explanation: The halogens have seven valence electrons and need just one more for an octet, so they form one bond.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the nitrogen atom in ammonia, NH3, have?
explanation: Nitrogen shares six of its valence electrons in three covalent bonds to hydrogen; its remaining two valence electrons form one nonbonding lone pair.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in water, H2O, have?
explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons. Two are used in its two O–H bonds, and the other four form two lone pairs, completing the octet.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons are there in chloromethane, CH3Cl?
explanation: Carbon uses all four of its valence electrons in bonds, and hydrogen has none left over. Chlorine uses one of its seven valence electrons in the C–Cl bond, leaving six as three lone pairs.

prompt: Phosphorus is in group 5A. How many hydrogen atoms does it bond to in phosphine?
explanation: Phosphorus has five valence electrons, so it needs to share three more to make an octet. It bonds to three hydrogen atoms, giving PH3.

prompt: Carbon forms four bonds. If a molecule has formula CH?Cl2, how many hydrogens does it contain?
explanation: Carbon forms four bonds. Two go to chlorine atoms, so the other two go to hydrogens: CH2Cl2.

prompt: Silicon is in the same group as carbon. What is the subscript ? in the likely formula SiF?
explanation: Like carbon, silicon has four valence electrons and forms four bonds. Each fluorine forms one bond, so the formula is SiF4.

prompt: In the likely formula CH3NH?, how many hydrogens are on the nitrogen?
explanation: Nitrogen forms three bonds. One goes to the CH3 carbon, so two go to hydrogens: CH3NH2 (methylamine).

prompt: Why can't an organic molecule have the formula C2H7?

choices.text: Two bonded carbons have room for at most six hydrogens
Carbon can't bond to another carbon
choices.why: Carbon atoms readily bond to one another, as in ethane, C2H6.

choices.text: Hydrogen forms two bonds
choices.why: Hydrogen forms only one bond.

choices.text: Seven is an odd number of atoms
choices.why: Many molecules have odd numbers of hydrogens, such as CH3Cl. The problem is valence.

explanation: Each carbon forms four bonds. In a two-carbon molecule one bond on each carbon joins the carbons, leaving 3 + 3 = 6 places for hydrogens (C2H6). A seventh hydrogen would give a carbon five bonds.

prompt: How does a Kekulé (line-bond) structure show a covalent bond?

choices.text: As a line between the two atoms, standing for the two shared electrons
As a pair of dots between the atoms
choices.why: That is how an electron-dot (Lewis) structure shows a bond.

choices.text: As a wedge
choices.why: Wedges show bonds coming toward the viewer in three-dimensional drawings.

choices.text: As the symbols written side by side with no line
choices.why: That is closer to a condensed structure; line-bond structures draw each bond as a line.

explanation: Even simpler than Lewis structures are Kekulé structures, or line-bond structures, in which the two-electron covalent bonds are indicated as lines drawn between atoms. Lone pairs are often left out of them, but they still have to be kept in mind.
